Bṛhaspati
(‘Lord of prayer’)
------------------------------------------
Bṛhaspati is a name that is often mentioned in the Hindu scriptures, right from the Ṛgveda up to the पुराणस् and the धर्मशास्त्रस्. Obviously there are several Bṛhaspatis, divine and human.
In the Ṛgveda he is described as the Lord of prayers and is identified with ब्रह्मणस्पति (2.23.1). He is considered as a devatā or a god. गणपति, the later paurāṇic deity, seems to have had his origin in this बृहस्पति-ब्रह्मणस्पति.
During the period of the epics and the पुराणस् he is described as a sage, the son of Aṅgīrasa. Being a person of great learningand wisdom and an expert in the performance of rituals, the gods in हेअवेन् under the leadership of Devendra, chose him as their गुरु or preceptor. शुक्राचार्य, the preceptor of the असुरस् or demons was his rival.
Tārā was his wife and the मोथेर् of बुध from चन्द्र, the मोओन्. बुध is one of the प्लनेत्स्.
He has many exploits attributed to him such as saving the worlds by assuming the form of अग्नि or fire, saving the honour of Śacīdevī, the consort of Devendra from being forced by the king नहुष, surreptitiously acquiring the knowledge of the rejuvenation of the dead through his son कच, misleading the असुरस् when Śukrā-cārya was away and so on.
Bṛhaspati is the presiding deity of the planet called गुरु or जुपितेर् and effects beneficial results. In the works on इचोनोग्रफ्य् he is described as a minor deity of splendid appearance, with rosary or with four arms, carrying a दण्ड (staff) and a कमण्डलु (water-pot) in addition. He is seated on a chariot drawn by eight horses.
Sometimes, बृहस्पति is mentioned as the originator of अथेइस्म्. This may have been based on the myth that he once disguised himself as शुक्राचार्य and taught अथेइस्म् and मतेरिअलिस्म् to the असुरस् to mislead them!
There is one more बृहस्पति, the writer of a dharmaśāstra, or अर्थशास्त्र. कौटिल्य (300 B.C.) has quoted several verses from his work. The Mahābhārata alludes to बृहस्पति who is said to have compressed into 3000 chapters the work on धर्म, अर्थ and काम composed originally by ब्रह्मा. The Vanaparva of the Mahābhārata speaks of a work called Bṛhaspatinīti.
This बृहस्पति is said to have advised the kings, the acquisition of only two vidyās—vartā (agriculture, trade and commerce) and दण्डनीति (statecraft including the laws governing च्रिमे अन्द् पुनिस्ह्मेन्त् as also the science of war).

Bṛhad-devatā
(‘[a] big work dealing with the] Vedic deities’)
------------------------------------------
The sage शौनक (500 B.C.) has done yeomen service to the preservation of the Vedic literature by composing ten works, generally classed as ‘anukramaṇīs’ (See ANUKRAMAṆĪ for details.) in which is included this celebrated work, Bṛhad-devatā. It is an index of the Vedic gods, more extensive than other similar works.
This treatise on the Vedic deities is in the form of verses in the anuṣṭubh meter spread over eight adhyāyas or chapters, corresponding to the eight aṣṭakas (the more ancient method of dividing the Ṛgveda) of the Ṛgveda. The first two chapters contain 125 verses of an introduc-tory nature which discuss several aspects of Vedic grammar useful in the analysis or interpretation of the Vedic words. Then the book takes up the difficult task of determining and describing the देवतास् or deities of the various sūktas of the Ṛgveda, often narrating interesting anecdotes also, related to those deities.
Some of the more ancient sages mentioned in this work are: Śākaṭāyana, यास्क, Śākapūṇi and Gālava.
Since an ‘Ācārya शौनक’ has been mentioned in this Bṛhad-devatā itself, some Western scholars opine that this work must have been composed by another person, probably his contemporary. But other scholars do not subscribe to this view.
See also ŚAUNAKA.

Bṛhatsaṁhitā
------------------------------------------
Jyautiṣa or अस्त्रोनोम्य् is Vedāṅga, a subsidiary science that helps in determining suitable times for the performance of वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्.
Over the centuries, ज्यौतिष evolved into a much larger and much more complicated science, embodying in itself, not onlyastronomy, but also अस्त्रोलोग्य्, the science that predicts the influence of the प्लनेत्स् and other heavenly bodies on human affairs.
One of the basic works on Hindu अस्त्रोलोग्य् is the Bṛhatsaṁhitā of Varāha-mihira (6th century A.D.). Though it deals mainly with अस्त्रोलोग्य्, it is quite encyclopaedic in its scope and includes several other branches of knowledge as geography, architecture, इचोनोग्रफ्य्, gem-therapy and so on. Each of these subjects has been treated, keeping in view its significance as an augury or its astrological effects. For instance, the section on rubies describes how one can know the quality of a gem, but it also gives the effects of wearing a good ruby.
Another interesting feature of this work is its 104th chapter. The various stanzas that deal with the astrological effects of the प्लनेत्स् are composed in different meters, the name of the meter itself being ingeniously included in the verse itself.
See also JYAUTIṢA and VARĀHAMIHIRA.

Bṛhad-धर्म-purāṇa
------------------------------------------
The पुराणस् (Hindu mythological lore) served two purposes. As the primary means of mass एदुचतिओन् they spread not only knowledge—both secular and sacred—but also wisdom and culture. In addition they also helped the society to preserve its history and hoary traditions.
The पुराणस् are generally classified into two groups: the mahāpurāṇas and the उपपुराणस्. Each group comprises 18 works.
The Bṛhad-धर्म-purāṇa is an upapurāṇa, probably compiled in the 13th century. It is more like a स्मृति or a dharmaśāstra than a purāṇa. Rites and practices of the various varṇas and āśramas, gifts, duties of women and others—these are some of the topics dealt with. The birth and sports of कृष्ण are also portrayed.
See also PURĀṆAS.

Bṛhajjātaka
------------------------------------------
Hindu अस्त्रोनोम्य् and its allied branch, अस्त्रोलोग्य्, are as old as the वेदस्. Called ‘Vedāṅga-ज्यौतिष’ or simply ‘Jyautiṣa’ it deals with the appropriate periods and timings for conducting the वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्.
Astrology deals more specifically with the influence of the स्तर्स् and प्लनेत्स् on human life, both at the individual and at the collective level.
Of the several ancient works (in Sanskrit) on अस्त्रोलोग्य्, the Bṛhajjātaka of वराहमिहिर (A.

) is generally consi-dered as the best and the most authoritative. It has 28 adhyāyas or chapters and 409 ślokas or verses in different metres. As the very name suggests, it deals mainly with jātakas or horoscopes of human beings. Of the four commentaries available now, that of भट्ट Utpala is considered the best.
The topics dealt with in the work are: the twelve rāśis or the ज़ोदिअचल् सिग्न्स्, the nine प्लनेत्स्, effects of the प्लनेत्स् at the time of conception on the person to be born, indications of early death, longe-vity of a child, lunar combinations, avocations as indicated by the प्लनेत्स्, miscellaneous planetary combinations, on evils, on female horoscopes, on death and on lost horoscopes.
In the last chapter the author apo-logises for any mistakes that may have crept in and also gives some information about himself. He was the son of a ब्राह्मण, Ādityadāsa by name, hailing from the village Kapittha. He got his एदुचतिओन् and knowledge from Savitṛ (the Sun-god). He lived in the court of उज्जयिनी in the province of Avantī.
See also BṚHATSAṀHITĀ and VARĀHA-MIHIRA.

Bṛhajjābālopaniṣad
------------------------------------------
The उपनिषद्स् are the foundation of the Vedānta philosophy. Apart from the ten उपनिषद्स्, considered as very ancient and canonical, there are a large number of other works, also designated as उपनिषद्स्. Most of these belong to a much later period and are obviously the creations of the master-minds of the various sects to further their own views. The Bṛhajjābālopaniṣad is one such, of the Śaivite group. Assigned to the Atharvaṇa-veda, it comprises 8 ब्राह्मणस् or chapters. The total number of mantras—in verses, interspersed with long passages in prose also—is 178.
The Upaniṣad is concerned mainly with भस्म or the holy ash, dear to शिव.
The sage Bhusuṇḍa was a great योगि but with a corvine body. Once प्रजापति entered into him in a subtle form and made him approach Kālāgni रुद्र (one of the several aspects of God शिव) with the question, ‘O Lord! Kindly tell me about the greatness of विभूति or the holy ash and रुद्राक्ष (the berry of the tree Elaeocarpus ganitrus).’
The reply of the Lord as given in the first ब्राह्मण may be briefly stated as follows: शिव has five faces: सद्योजात, वामदेव, अघोर, Tatpuruṣa and ईशान. From these emanated five divine cows named Nandā, Bhadrā, सुरभि, Suśīlā and Citravarṇā, all of different colours. The holy ashes prepared out of the dungs of these cows are known as—vibhūti, bhasita, भस्म, kṣāra and rakṣā.
The second ब्राह्मण starts with the question of Bhusuṇḍi about the rules concerning bhasmasnāna or a bath with the holy ash. The Lord replies by stating that this world itself is भस्म and it assumes several forms by being their antarātman or the inner Self. Here भस्म is identified with the Lord himself since he alone is left when the super-imposed world is negated, even as भस्म or ash is left when everything is consumed in the fire.
The world is called ‘agnīṣomātmaka’ since अग्नि (the fire element) and सोम (the मोओन् element responsible for रस or essence or juices) are its components in the cosmic sense. अग्नि and सोम are also identified with the शिव and शक्ति. Hence the whole world is a product of the combination of शिव and शक्ति. One who realises that शिव and शक्ति are identical and also his own oneness with them, attains अमृतत्व or इम्मोर्तलित्य्.
The third ब्राह्मण describes the process of preparing the विभूति or the holy ash. The dung of which types of cows is to be selected and which to be avoided is stated first. After preparing small balls of the dung and drying them in the sun, they have to be offered into the fire with the appropriate mantras. The भस्म or ash collected should then be scented with certain dry powders, uttering the mantras as stated in the work.
The भस्म should then be applied all over the body, from head to feet, chanting the Pañcabrahma-mantras (Mahānārāyaṇopaniṣad 17 to 21) while doing so.
The fourth ब्राह्मण states the times of the day—like dawn, dusk and night—when भस्म can be applied. This भस्म should be applied as three lines on the forehead, with the three middle fingers after mixing it with the water from a conch. While applying it, one should think of the three aspects of God, ब्रह्मा, विष्णु and शिव. The भस्म can be applied on other parts of the body also, like the chest, throat and nose.
The fifth ब्राह्मण gives some more details concerning the wearing of भस्म on the forehead and other parts of the body. The three lines have to be mentally identified with the three Vedas—the Sāmaveda, the Yajurveda and the Ṛgveda—in that order from the top to the bottom. The members of the three varṇas (brāhmaṇas, kṣattriyas and vaiśyas) should use the भस्म of the गार्हपत्य fire used for the अग्निहोत्र sacrifice. The avadhūtas—the saints who have transcended the वर्ण and आश्रम system—should wear the ashes gathered from the च्रेमतिओन् ground. The ashes obtained from a शिव temple are sacred for all, without any distinction.
This is then followed by an eulogy of wearing the tripuṇḍra—the three lines drawn with the bhasma—by narrating the fruits that will accrue to the wearer. Then comes a castigation in strong terms, of those who have abandoned wearing the भस्म or who deride and harass the votaries that wear it.
The greatness and the miraculous powers of भस्म are recounted by the next, the sixth, ब्राह्मण. It can revive even dead persons if sprinkled upon the bodies with the Mṛtyuñjaya-mantra. It can destroy the sins of even the vilest ones and can grant knowledge even to Hari or विष्णु! The section ends with further eulogies of the knowledge taught here, called Bṛhajjābālavidyā.
The seventh ब्राह्मण is almost a revision of the earlier section. It also describes the birth of the रुद्राक्ष beads (the berries of the tree Elaeocarpus ganitrus) and the mode of wearing them. These beads were born out of the eyes (akṣa or akṣi) of रुद्र, and hence the name रुद्राक्ष. One who wears them on his body attains infinite merit.
The last chapter—the eighth brāh-maṇa—states the results of reciting this Upaniṣad such as attaining purity, the capacity to assert the power of the elemental forces like fire and wind, conquest of death and all the worlds, as also getting the knowledge of all sciences. After death, the reciter attains the Supreme.
See also BHASMAJĀBĀLOPANIṢAD.

Bṛhadīśvara Temple
(‘Temple of the Great Lord’)
------------------------------------------
Belief in God is a basic human trait. Though this God may be the infinite cosmic spirit, the human being, encased as he is, in a limited frame and a limited मिन्द्, can think of him only in a place of worship or in a temple.
Hindu temples are a very ancient institution. Their development has been spread over several centuries. Though the earliest permanent structures built out of stone and bricks that have withstood the vagaries of time have been assigned to the 4th century A.D., icons of gods and goddesses have been discovered even in the हरप्प-Mohenjodaro excavations (2500 B.C.) suggesting the possibility of existence of places of worship.
In the history of the development of the हिन्दु तेम्प्लेस्, the Coḷā period (A.

-1200) is one of the golden periods. The बृहदीश्वर तेम्प्ले of Tañjāvūr (also spelt as Tanjore) in Tamil Nadu is a remarkable structure, perhaps the biggest and the best, belonging to this period. It was built by Rājarāja the First (reign A.

-1013).
The story goes that Rājarāja was a victim of black leprosy due to the sins committed in an earlier life as a hunter. To expiate the sins and to get rid of the disease, he was commanded by his गुरु हरदत्त to build a temple for शिव after getting a लिङ्ग (emblem of शिव) from the river नर्मदा. When the king went to the river and got the लिङ्ग out of water, it started growing bigger and bigger. Hence the name Bṛhadīśvara (bṛhat = big or large). The temple took twelve years to build and was consecrated during A.

. The official name given to the लिङ्ग or the deity is राजराजेश्वर.
The temple complex is situated in the southern half of a small fort and is surrounded by a moat on the east and the west. Apart from the main temple, the complex contains temples of देवी called Bṛhannāyakī, सुब्रह्मण्य, गणेश, नवग्रहस् and a number of liṅgas estimated around 252.
The length and width of the actual temple structure is 45.5 metres (150 ft.) and 27 metres (90 ft.).
The most striking feature of this temple is its विमान or towered sanctuary which rises perpendicularly from a 15 metre (50 ft.) high square base and then tapers off to a total height of 65 metres (216 ft.). There are fourteen storeys, with small pillars, pretty balcony windows and beautiful images carved thereon. The कलश or finial is 3.8 metres (12.5 ft.) high and weighs 80 tonnes.
The लिङ्ग itself is quite massive, both in diameter and in height.
Nandi, the mount of शिव, placed in front is also of generous proportions, measuring nearly 6 metres (20 ft.) in length and 3.6 metres (12 ft.) in height. It is said to be the second biggest in India, the one at लेपाक्षि (in Andhra Pradesh) being the biggest.
The corridor of circumambulation just outside the sanctum sanctorum has fresco paintings depicting stories and incidents from Hindu म्य्थोलोग्य्.
Another temple in the campus, dedicated to सुब्रह्मण्य or कार्त्तिकेय (son of शिव) deserves our attention due to its being an exquisite piece of architecture. The stone carvings of elaborate patterns are perfect. Its विमान (tower over the shrine) rises to a height of 16.5 metres (55 ft.). It was probably built around A.

by the Naik dynasty.
The religious rituals of the temple are according to the Mukuṭāgama and the ब्रह्मोत्सव, the chief festival, is conducted for 18 days during April-May.

Bṛhannalā
------------------------------------------
This is the name that अर्जुन, the great Pāṇḍava hero, assumed when he had to live in the palace of the king विराट for one year as a eunuch, among the ladies of the palace, teaching them मुसिच् and dancing.
When the Kauravas attacked विराट’s capital and seized the palace cows, बृहन्नला became the charioteer of Uttara-कुमार, the son of विराट. उत्तरकुमार went to the battlefield to repulse the attack but was too frightened to fight. So, बृहन्नला had to reveal his identity and do the fighting himself.
Arjuna had once been cursed to become a eunuch, by the nymph ऊर्वशी since he had spurned, though respectfully, her amorous advances. The curse came in handy during the one year period the Pāṇḍavas had to live incognito as per the accord with the Kauravas, after they had been defeated in the game of dice.
See also ARJUNA.

Bṛhan-nāradīya-purāṇa
------------------------------------------
Purāṇas or the mythological works of हिन्दुइस्म् serve several purposes. They amplify and expound the truths contained in the वेदस्. They give us a glimpse of the contemporary history and culture. They also prescribe a code of conduct to be followed by all, for the welfare of the society. More often they give detailed accounts of several sciences like town-planning, architecture, sculpture, medical sciences or religious rites motivated by the desire for worldly well-being, since that was their way of educating the public.
These पुराणस् are usually classified into two groups: the Mahāpurāṇas and the उपपुराणस्. Each group is said to contain 18 works and all are ascribed by tradition to the sage वेदव्यास.
The Bṛhan-nāradīya-purāṇa is classed among the minor पुराणस् and is assigned to the period A.

. It is a sectarian work of the Vaiṣnava schools. One of the printed versions comprises 3600 verses in 38 chapters.
Sometimes this purāṇa has been considered as the first part of the Nāradīya-purāṇa itself.
Praise of विष्णु and of भक्ति, geo-graphy of India, story of सगर, गङ्गा-māhātmya, a few vratas (religious vows and rites), varṇāśrama-dharmas and śrāddha (obsequial ceremonies)—these are the general contents of this purāṇa.
See also PURĀṆAS.

Bṛhat-पराशर-saṁhitā
(‘A big collection of verses of पराशर’)
------------------------------------------
Medieval, and even modern, Hindu practices depend much upon the धर्म-śāstras, works that generally deal with आचार and vyavahāra, personal and social conduct.-
One such work, though not an ancient one wielding greater authority, is the Bṛhat-पराशर-saṁhitā. It appears to be a recast of an earlier work, the Parāśara Smṛti.
Said to have been imparted by the sage पराशर to Suvrata, it contains about 3000 verses divided into 12 chapters.
The subject matter contains the following topics: the sphere of the āryas; the six daily karmas like bath, सन्ध्या, जप, worship of gods and honouring guests; the गायत्री मन्त्र; the duties of the various varṇas and āśramas; forms of मर्रिअगे and connected topics; on gifts; śrāddha or after-death ceremonies; prāyaścittas or expiations; rites for propitiating deities like गणेश and रुद्र; some aspects of योग like प्राणायाम and so on.
See also DHARMAŚĀSTRAS and PARĀŚARA.

Bṛhatī
(‘the big one’)
------------------------------------------
The बृहती is a well-known छन्दस् or meter of Vedic Saṁhitās. Out of 14 such Vedic meters, it occupies the 4th place. It has 4 pādas or quarters, with 9 letters in each pāda. According to the sage शौनक, as mentioned in his Chando’nu-kramaṇī, there are 181 mantras in the Ṛgveda Saṁhitā composed in the Bṛhati metre.
Bṛhatī is also the name of a well-known commentary by प्रभाकर (8th century) on the Śābara-bhāṣya, which itself is a commentary by Śabara (57 B.C.) on the famous Mīmāṁsāsūtras of जैमिनि (200 B. C.).

Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
Introduction
Out of the three basic scriptures of हिन्दुइस्म् known as the प्रस्थानत्रय, the उपनिषद्स् rank first. In the group of the ten उपनिषद्स् the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and the Chāndogya occupy a unique place since they not only delineate the fundamental principles of Vedānta but also describe a number of upāsanās or meditations, technically called Vidyās.
The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, as its very name suggests, is quite a large work (bṛhad = large, big) and forms an integral part of the well-known Śatapatha Brāh-maṇa which itself belongs to the Śukla Yajurveda. The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa has two recensions—the Kāṇva and the Mādhyandina. The former has 17 kāṇḍas or sections whereas the latter has only 14. The six adhyāyas or chapters of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka actually form chapters 3 to 8 of the 17th kāṇḍa in the Kāṇva recension and chapters 4 to 9 of the 14th kāṇḍa of the Mādhyandina recension.
The adhyāyas are divided into khaṇḍas or ब्राह्मणस्, which again are subdivided into kaṇḍikās (similar to mantras). There are 435 kaṇḍikās distri-buted among the 47 ब्राह्मणस् of the 6 adhyāyas of this Upaniṣad.
There is another way of dividing this Upaniṣad. The first two adhyāyas form the Madhukāṇḍa, the middle two, the Munikāṇḍa or the Yājñavalkyakāṇḍa and the last two, Khilakāṇḍa. These kāṇḍas respectively deal with upadeśa (the teaching), upapatti (the argument) and upāsanā (the meditations and rites).
By far, the Munikāṇḍa, which accounts for almost half the number of the kaṇḍikās, is the most important part of this Upaniṣad. The sage याज्ञवल्क्य, who is the principal person that appears here, has expounded brilliantly the philo-sophy of आत्मन्/Brahman as also several subtle aspects of related teachings. He can easily be classified among the greatest thinkers of the world of any age.
A chapterwise summary of the work may now be attempted.
First Chapter
The first ब्राह्मण known as the Aśva-brāhmaṇa, describes a special process of meditation wherein the various aspects of प्रजापति, the Creator, like kāla (time), लोक (the various worlds) and devatā (the various deities) are advised to be superimposed on the different limbs of the horse chosen for the अश्वमेध (horse-sacrifice). This can transform—in a spiritual sense—the horse into प्रजापति himself. The ritual of the अश्वमेध itself can lead the performer to ब्रह्मलोक or the world of ब्रह्मा, also known as हिरण्यगर्भ. Though only kings are competent to perform this sacrifice, even others can attain to the same result by imagining themselves to be the horse and superposing the various items on themselves as described.
Agni-brāhmaṇa is the second section of this chapter. It deals with the manifestation of अग्नि or fire from प्रजापति and the method of contemplation on it as प्रजापति himself. This leads to the fruit of mṛtyujaya or conquest of death.
The third is the Udgītha-brāhmaṇa. The उद्गीथ is the second and the most important part of a सामन् sung by the priest ugdātṛ in a सोम sacrifice. In this ब्राह्मण, the importance of प्राण, the vital force, has been brought out by an allegorical story. The देवस् or gods wanted to conquer the असुरस् or demons by performing the ज्योतिष्टोम sacrifice. They employed sense-organs like the speech, the eye, the nose, and also the मिन्द् to sing the उद्गीथ for them. The असुरस्, however, succeeded in contaminating them through selfishness, thereby defeating the purpose of the देवस्. However, when these असुरस् rushed towards the प्राण, the chief vital force, they were destroyed. By meditating on one’s प्राण, which is not only the real power behind the sense-organs but also the essence of the वेदस् and a replica of the cosmic प्राण (also known as प्रजापति or हिरण्यगर्भ) one can attain to the world of प्रजापति. The speciality of this upāsanā or meditation is that it does not involve any rites or rituals.
The fourth khaṇḍa is known as the Puruṣavidha-brāhmaṇa. Before च्रेअतिओन्, the entire universe was within the body of पुरुष or प्रजापति or विराज्, undifferenti-ated from him. He desired for a mate. As a result of his will, he projected out of himself another entity which split into two, the male part being मनु and the female Śatarūpā. By their union, not only in the human form, but also in various other forms, all the living beings, up to an ant, were created. He, however, remained as he was, unaffected. He then realized that the created universe of beings was also himself. Later, he created the gods like अग्नि.
Since the पुरुष, the Supreme Self, has entered into the whole च्रेअतिओन् and exists in it like a sword in its sheath or fire in the wood, it is he who is being manifested through all the activities of the body-मिन्द् complex. However, the activities like speaking and the names like speech, are only nomenclatures born out of the various types of functioning. He is the inmost self in us and is unaffected by the sense of doership or actions or their fruits, which have been superimposed on him by अविद्या or इग्नोरन्चे of his real nature. The sage वामदेव and many others like him, realized that they were in the ultimate analysis, the Supreme Self.
Then comes a classification of the gods. अग्नि is ब्राह्मण. इन्द्र, वरुण, सोम, यम and ईशान are kṣattriyas. वसुस्, Rudras and Ādityas are vaiśyas. पूषन् is a śūdra. The human beings were born out of these four classes of gods. The पुरुष or the Supreme Being also created धर्म or righteousness (the Cosmic Law) to regulate them all. However, it is declared that an ajñāni or an ignorant person becomes an object of enjoyment for all. These ignorant ones are advised to discharge their debts to the gods and the others through the पञ्चयज्ञस् or the five daily sacrifices. The Upaniṣad also says that it is desire that binds a person and it is meditation on the आत्मन् or the Self alone that can deliver him. One who fails in this has to suffer much.
The next khaṇḍa is known as the Saptānna-brāhmaṇa, the ब्राह्मण of seven foods. The first अन्न or ड़ोओद् is the usual physical ड़ोओद् upon which all living beings sustain themselves. Human beings have to consume ड़ोओद् so that they can perform the prescribed religious rites which can give them the unseen results later on. If they do not perform these rites, they will be eating only sin. The second and the third annas are the huta and the prahuta sacrificial oblations and gifts given during the sacrifices. They are sometimes, identified with the two sacrifices Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa, meant for the gods. Milk is the fourth अन्न, specially meant for the animals.
The last three annas or foods, were kept by प्रजापति for himself. They are: vāk (speech), मनस् (mind) and प्राण (vital force). Since they help him to create the worlds and sustain them, they are called ‘anna’. These three are then identi-fied with the three worlds, the three वेदस्, the three beings (gods, manes and human beings) and so on. In fact they comprise the whole world. One who meditates upon them as limited, attains the finite world. If he meditates upon them as unlimited, he obtains the infinite world.
This प्रजापति or the हिरण्यगर्भ is himself the time. The Upaniṣad des-cribes how the various organs like vāk or speech, competed against one another but were overcome by fatigue. However, प्राण or the vital force was not affected by it. Hence, the organs identified themselves with it and became immortal. Among the gods like अग्नि (fire), आदित्य (Sun) and चन्द्र (Moon), only वायु (air), the cosmic counterpart of प्राण, could sustain itself in its work. If a person can meditate on the organs like speech which exist in all living beings and the elements like fire, which exist in this world, as identified with his own Self, he attains identity with हिरण्यगर्भ and live in his world.
The sixth and the last khaṇḍa, which is sometimes called the Uktha-brāhmaṇa, declares that the whole universe is nothing but nāma (name), rūpa (form) and कर्म (action). Like the three mutually supporting sticks, these three support one another and also help in manifesting one another. Since this universe is only an उपाधि or limiting adjunct to परमात्मन् (the Supreme Self), anyone who is interested in it, will not be inclined to meditate on him.
Second Chapter
This chapter, comprising six brāhma-ṇas, is more directly concerned with ātma-tattva or the knowledge of the आत्मन्. The well-known discourse by the great sage याज्ञवल्क्य to his wife Maitreyī—which, incidentally, appears in the fourth chapter also, though shorter—forms the core of this chapter.
The first ब्राह्मण known as the Ajātaśatru-brāhmaṇa starts with the legend of बालाकि the proud one, a descendant of गर्ग and अजातशत्रु, the king of काशी. बालाकि proposed to अजातशत्रु to teach ब्रह्मन्. However, what he taught was elementary and concerned only with the conditioned ब्रह्मन्, like the Being resid-ing in the sun, the मोओन्, the lightning, the ether, the air and so on. But अजातशत्रु knew better. He had realized the uncondi-tioned ब्रह्मन्. So, he taught this to बालाकि. In deep sleep, all the sense organs like speech, are absorbed in their sources, the individual Self is merged in the Supreme Self, the unconditioned ब्रह्मन्. It then resembles a child or a great king or a worthy ब्राह्मण, having reached the acme of bliss. The teaching ends with a statement that all the beings, all the worlds and all the gods emerge out of the आत्मन्, the Supreme Being, even as sparks spring from fire.
The next the Śiśu-brāhmaṇa and it speaks of the प्राण or the vital force as a calf. Its body is its abode, the head is its special place, the vigour generated by ड़ोओद् and drink is its post and the ड़ोओद् itself is its tether. Seven deities like रुद्र and आदित्य are praising this प्राण. One who knows thus, will never be without ड़ोओद्.
The third is the Mūrtāmūrta-brāh-maṇa and it is devoted to the description of the two forms of ब्रह्मन्. One form is gross, mortal, limited and perceptible. The other is subtle, immortal, unlimited and imperceptible. By superimposing these two forms, the Supreme ब्रह्मन् is made conceivable. The words ‘neti, नेति’ (‘not this, not this’) deny all limitations to ब्रह्मन् and reveal its essential nature.
Next comes the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa which starts with the story of याज्ञवल्क्य and his two wives, मैत्रेयी and Kātyā-yanī. It stresses the need for सṁन्यास or monastic life, to attain the Self. The sage याज्ञवल्क्य, intending to embrace the monastic life, wants to divide his wealth between the two wives. However, मैत्रेयी, after learning that the wealth, and the Vedic rites performed with the help of wealth, cannot give her इम्मोर्तलित्य्, rejects the offer of wealth and opts for आत्मज्ञान or the knowledge of the Self. याज्ञवल्क्य responds by teaching her that all the beings here like the husband or the wife or the children, as also wealth or the various worlds or the gods are dear to us only because of the आत्मन् or the Self in them and not by themselves. This आत्मन् has to be heard of (from a qualified teacher), reflected upon and meditated upon—these three being called śravaṇa, मनन and nidi-dhyāsana—in order to be realized. As it is not possible to grasp the special sources of a drum or a conch or a lute without the grasping of sound in general, it is not possible to perceive anything in this world as different from ब्रह्मन्, its basic reality. याज्ञवल्क्य further asserts that even the वेदस् have emerged out of it and that it exists in everything as homogeneous चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, even as salt exists everywhere in the water in which it has been dissolved. Perception of duality in this world is only apparent and has been caused by अविद्या or इग्नोरन्चे of the Reality.
Madhu-brāhmaṇa, the fifth section, sums up the import of the first two chapters. There is an elaborate account of the आत्मन् or the Self which is the ruler and the king of all beings. Even as spokes are fixed in the nave and the rim of a chariot wheel, so are all beings, all gods and all worlds are fixed in the Supreme Self. The Sage Dadhyaṅ Ātharvaṇa taught this knowledge of the Self to the two Aśvins—the twin gods—through a temporary equine head. The ब्राह्मण ends with the essential teaching of all the Vedānta texts, viz., that the Self, though one, is perceived as manifold through māyā his inscrutable power.
Vaṁśa-brāhmaṇa, the last section of this chapter, gives the line of teachers beginning with हिरण्यगर्भ.
Third Chapter
Whereas the Madhukāṇḍa, comprising the first two chapters dealt with upadeśa or āgama (the teachings), the Munikāṇḍa (also called Yājñavalkīya-kāṇḍa) consisting of the third and the fourth chapters, strengthens it through upapatti or yukti, or reasoning. There are nine ब्राह्मणस् in the third chapter.
The first is the Aśvala-brāhmaṇa. It starts with an interesting story. जनक Vaideha, the great king, had just completed a big sacrifice—the Bahudakṣiṇa—to participate in which, a large number of ब्राह्मणस् from the countries of कुरु and Pañcāla had come. The king proposed to give away as a gift, a thousand cows on the horns of each of which had been tied ten gold coins, to the Brahmiṣṭha (the most learned in ब्रह्मन् or the वेदस्) among them. Though none of the assembled dared to accept the challenge, याज्ञवल्क्य did. He even ordered his disciple Sāmaśrava to drive the cattle home! Naturally the assembly fell into a rage and all started questioning him. Aśvala who was the first to pose eight questions to him, was easily vanquished by the satisfactory replies of याज्ञवल्क्य.
The Ārtabhāga-brāhmaṇa, the next section, starts with another Vedic scholar, Ārtabhāga, shooting six questions at याज्ञवल्क्य who answers them all to the satisfaction of the questioner. The last of these questions deals with the problem of the destination of the सोउल् of a dead person. याज्ञवल्क्य takes Ārtabhāga to a secluded place and the two finally conclude that it is कर्म that decides the future life of the सोउल् of a dead person. Good कर्म leads to noble births and bad कर्म to ignoble ones.
Bhujyu-brāhmaṇa, the third, states that even the best of karmas or rites results in transmigration and that even karmas accompanied by upāsanā or meditation cannot give मोक्ष or freedom.
The fourth is the Uṣasta-brāhmaṇa. Uṣasta questions याज्ञवल्क्य to tell him about ब्रह्मन् which is sākṣāt (immediate) and aparokṣāt (direct). याज्ञवल्क्य replies that it is the आत्मन् that works in the body through the five prāṇas or vital-airs. It is the seer and the knower and hence it cannot be seen or known like an external object.
The Kahola-brāhmaṇa follows next. A further description of the आत्मन् is given here, as beyond hunger, thirst, sorrow, delusion, old-age and death. The wise ones realize this आत्मन् and give up their desire for progeny, wealth and meritorious worlds. A realized सोउल् is a realized सोउल् irrespective of his conduct. His brahma-ज्ञान or knowledge of ब्रह्मन् never ceases.
The sixth section, named Gārgī-brāhmaṇa, deals with the questions posed by Gārgī, the daughter of Vacaknu, and the ready answers given by याज्ञवल्क्य. The questions concerned with the relative subtlety of the पञ्चभूतस् or the five elements as also the worlds right up to the ब्रह्मलोक, the abode of ब्रह्मन्. When she asks, ‘By what is the Brahma-लोक pervaded?’ याज्ञवल्क्य warns her not to proceed further since the nature of ब्रह्मन् can be known only through the scriptures and the preceptor and never through लोगिच् or inference.
The Antaryāmi-brāhmaṇa is the seventh in the series. It is now the turn of उद्दालक आरुणि to question Yājña-valkya. It concerns the ‘antaratama-sūtra’ or the inmost thread that passes through all the worlds and all the beings, holding them together. उद्दालक also asks about the अन्तर्यामिन्, the Being that dwells in all and controls them all. याज्ञवल्क्य replies that वायु is that sūtra or thread. It is the आत्मन् that indwells all the worlds and all the beings. He resides in them and controls them whereas they know him not. He is the sākṣin or the eternal witness, the śrotṛ or the listener, the mantṛ or the thinker and the jñātṛ or the knower. However, he is not the object of चोग्नितिओन् for any of the senses. He is the immortal आत्मन्. All else is perishable.
This is followed by the Akṣara-ब्राह्मण, the eighth section, wherein Gārgī puts two questions to याज्ञवल्क्य. The first question is: ‘What pervades that (the sūtra) which is above हेअवेन् and below the earth as well as between them, and which was, is and will be?’ Yājña-valkya replies that it is आकाश, the unmanifested ether. In reply to her next question as to what pervades this आकाश also, he answers that it is अक्षर, the indestructible. He describes it through several words revealing its unique qualities: It is asthūla (not gross), anaṇu (not fine), ahrasva (not short), adīrgha (not long), atamaḥ (not darkness), anākāśam (not ether), acakṣuṣkam (without eyes), aprāṇam (without the vital force), amanaḥ (without मिन्द्) and so on.
It can be described only by such negative attributes since it can never be apprehended either by the senses or by the मिन्द्.
Yājñavalkya further avers that, verily under the command of this अक्षर (the Absolute) only the sun, the मोओन् and all the heavenly bodies are held in their positions and perform their allotted duties. Rivers and mountains, quarters and directions and even time itself, keep to their duties. It is by the rule of this very Absolute that the lives of the human beings and the gods in हेअवेन् are being regulated.
He concludes by saying that the performance of any rite or ritual without knowing this अक्षर is a waste and that the condition of one who leaves this world without realizing this अक्षर will be miserable. But the one who leaves this world after knowing this अक्षर will be a knower of ब्रह्मन्.
Śākalya-brāhmaṇa is the last section of this chapter . It conveys the immediacy and directness of ब्रह्मन् by a reference to the different enumerations of the gods who are ruled by it. In reply to शाकल्य’s question about the number of gods याज्ञवल्क्य says that though there are tens or hundreds or thousands of gods they are the manifestations of but one God, हिरण्यगर्भ, who is the cosmic aspect of प्राण or the vital force. This God is one and at the same time, the many. Hence, when the upāsaka (the worshipper) gets identified with हिरण्यगर्भ, he becomes all, the Self of all.
Finally याज्ञवल्क्य asks the assembled ब्राह्मणस् whether they know the root from which a dead person is reborn, even as a tree that is cut off, springs up again from the original root. They were ignorant of it. The Upaniṣad itself declares that this root is ब्रह्मन्, the चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् and the bliss, the ultimate resort of all the human beings, be they the performers of rituals or the knower of ब्रह्मन्.
Fourth Chapter
This chapter comprises six ब्राह्मणस्. In the first, known as the Ṣaḍācārya-brāhmaṇa, याज्ञवल्क्य poses some questions to the king जनक Vaideha. The king in his reply states the characteristics of ब्रह्मन् as he had learnt from six of his teachers. He posits अग्नि, वायु, आदित्य, Digdevatā, चन्द्र and प्रजापति, the presiding deities of speech, vital air, eyes, ears, मिन्द् and intellect, as ब्रह्मन्. याज्ञवल्क्य rules them out as only partial manifestations of ब्रह्मन्.
In the Kūrca-brāhmaṇa, the second, याज्ञवल्क्य describes the avasthātraya or the three states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् which the embodied आत्मन् experiences. जाग्रत् (waking state), स्वप्न (dream state) and सुषुप्ति (deep-sleep state) are the three states and the सोउल् while associated with these three states is designated as Viśva (or वैश्वानर), तैजस and प्राज्ञ. Though the terms used in this section are different, the interpretation given by the commentators leads us to this conclusion.
The third section is the Jyotir-brāhmaṇa, a fairly voluminous one, comprising 38 kaṇḍikas. The avasthātraya or the three states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, mentioned in the previous ब्राह्मण, is discussed in detail through yukti or लोगिच् and reasoning. For an ordinary human being endowed with the body and the senses, what is it that acts as a jyoti or light?—This is the question that जनक repeatedly asks याज्ञवल्क्य. याज्ञवल्क्य lists them one by one as: the sun, the मोओन्, fire, speech and आत्मन् or the Self. When questioned about this आत्मन्, associ-ated with the body and the senses, याज्ञवल्क्य says that as a large fish swims alternately to both banks of a river, so this आत्मन्, simulating the intellect, moves between the dream world and the waking world. Since the intellect is transparent and next to the आत्मन्, it easily reflects the चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् of the latter. Like a crystal glowing in the light of a lamp, the intellect also, though bereft of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, appears to shine by the light or चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् of the आत्मन्, which alone is self-luminous. in fact the luminaries like the sun and the मोओन् are able to shine only by the light of the आत्मन्.
Then follows the conception of dream according to the Vedānta. In the dream state, the Self puts aside the gross body of the waking state and creates a dream-body comprising the impressions of the waking state. द्रेअम्स् are not new experi-ences of the waking state. Sometimes they may reflect the experiences of past lives also. The objects of the dream state are then and there created by the मिन्द्. Though the Self is dreaming, he has no direct connection with the physical body. Hence it is not advisable to suddenly wake up a sleeping person as that may endanger his life or senses. In dream, the Self merely witnesses the results of good and bad actions but does not actually experience them or do anything.
The आत्मन् or the Self then enters the samprasāda or the सुषुप्ति state, the state of deep-sleep. He enjoys supreme peace and bliss in this state, since he has merged himself in the Supreme Self. This is the nearest approximation to the state of ब्रह्मन्. However, अविद्या or इग्नोरन्चे does persist even in that state, though in an unmanifested form.
Then follows a description of the sufferings of an aged or diseased body in order to rouse the spirit of renunciation in us. When the Self leaves the present body it takes up another, made ready by its own past work. This passing of the Self is analogous to the return of man from the dream to the waking state.
The Śārīraka-brāhmaṇa, the fourth section, gives a detailed description of the transmigration of the जीव or the Self. At the time of death it withdraws its sense-organs and comes to the heart. It then exits through one of the parts of the body. The potential results of upāsanā (meditation), कर्म (good and bad deeds) and vāsanās (past impressions) follow the जीव in its onward journey. It creates for itself a new body, even as the goldsmith prepares ornaments out of gold. Once the results of past deeds are exhausted, it returns to this world for new work. It should be noted that only a person with desires and cravings transmigrates and not the one who has no cravings. The latter is merged in ब्रह्मन्, after casting off his body even as a snake casts off its slough. The knowers of ब्रह्मन् alone become immortal. The others are miserable.
There is no duality or multiplicity in ब्रह्मन्. One who sees it otherwise transmigrates from death to death. The seeker of ब्रह्मन् should not reflect on many words which only cause exhaustion to the vocal cords. He should abjure all vain talk.
Other teachings given in this section are: The आत्मन् in reality, is unaffected by good or bad deeds. Knowledge of this आत्मन् alone can make a being a ‘muni’ or a sage. Seekers of लिबेरतिओन् desire only the आत्मन् and not the worlds of men, of the manes or of the gods. Hence they renounce their hearth and home and become मोन्क्स्. The आत्मन् cannot be defined in positive terms. At best it can be described negatively as ‘neti’ (‘not this’). The knower of the आत्मन् is never beset with the thoughts of rewards or punishments for his past actions. He is ever controlled, serene and free from desires. He sees the आत्मन् in himself and all else also as his own Self. He is free from all doubts and evils, ever blessed and absolutely fearless.
The fifth brāhmaṇa—the Maitreyi-brāhmaṇa—is, for all practical purposes, a repetition of 2.4. The last section—the Vaṁśa-brāhmaṇa—traces the genealogy of the ācāryas or the teachers. As in the Madhukāṇḍa, here also, हिरण्यगर्भ is the primeval teacher.
Fifth Chapter
With this, begins the Khilakāṇḍa, the ‘supplementary book’. The fifth chapter introduces some auxiliary meditations which do not conflict with the rites but lead to worldly well-being and also क्रममुक्ति or gradual लिबेरतिओन्.
The first ब्राह्मण starts with the well-known śāntimantra (peace-chant) ‘pūrṇamadaḥ.’ The infinite universe has come out of the infinite ब्रह्मन्. Even after realizing its identity with ब्रह्मन्, ब्रह्मन् alone is left, because the universe as sopādhika or conditioned ब्रह्मन् has no real existence. The latter half deals with praṇavopāsana or meditation on ब्रह्मन् with the प्रणव or ओङ्कार.
Prājāpatya-brāhmaṇa, the second, prescribes the cultivation of the three qualities of दम (self-control), दान (giving gifts) and दया (showing compassion) as a part of upāsanā or meditation by means of an interesting parable.
The third is the Hṛdaya-brāhmaṇa which eulogises the heart, the seat of the intellect. The fourth and the fifth brāh-maṇas enjoin meditations on the हृदय-ब्रह्मन् as सत्य (the Truth) and its eulogy. Meditations on the different parts of its body are also described. The अक्षिपुरुष (the ocular being) or the जीव and the ādityapuruṣa or the solar being are aspects of सत्य-ब्रह्मन्. At the time of death, the solar being withdraws his rays and hence the dying man sees the sun as an orb without its rays.
The sixth called Mano-brāhmaṇa, enjoins a meditations on vidyut (lightning) and vāk (speech or the वेदस्) as ब्रह्मन्. The ninth recommends meditation on अग्नि or fire as वैश्वानर or विराज्. The tenth section known as the Gati-brāhmaṇa des-cribes the goals of the above meditations, which is, residence in ब्रह्मलोक throughout the life-time of हिरण्यगर्भ. Tapo-brāhmaṇa, the eleventh, advises us to look upon illness or being carried for the funeral after death, as a तपस् or penance, since it can destroy our sins. The twelfth section enjoins that अन्न (food) and प्राण (vital force) should be meditated upon as ब्रह्मन्. The thirteenth ब्राह्मण recommends meditations on the प्राण as uktha (a recitation connected with सोम-याग), yajus, सामन् and kṣattra (the healer).
The Gāyatrī-brāhmaṇa, the fourteenth, describes a meditation on ब्रह्मन् as possessing the गायत्री as the उपाधि or limiting adjunct. The four pādas or quarters of the गायत्री are to be identified respectively with the three worlds, the three वेदस्, the three prāṇas or vital-airs and आदित्य or the sun. This will result in various divine fruits.
The last section contains a prayer to आदित्य or the Sun and अग्नि or the fire by a dying man, who has combined meditation with rites (jñāna-कर्म-samuccaya), for the removal of the obstacles to his journey on the उत्तरायण or the northern path, after death.
Sixth Chapter
There are six ब्राह्मणस् in this chapter. Prāṇasaṁvāda-brāhmaṇa, the first one, demonstrates through an allegory that the प्राण or the vital force, is the eldest and the best of all organs. Once, a dispute arose among the sense-organs like the eye and the speech, as to which of them was the greatest. प्रजापति when approached by them for the adjudication, ruled that the greatest among them was that organ by whose departure the body would be rendered more impure. The departure of vāk (speech), चक्षुस् (the eyes), śrotra (the ears), retas (organ of generation) and मनस् (the मिन्द्), one by one, did not make the body more impure. It continued to live. But, when प्राण (also called mukhyaprāṇa) tried to depart, all the other organs also were pulled out of their places of residence. Hence it was decided that the प्राण or the vital force was the best.
The second is the Karmavipāka-brāhmaṇa which teaches the Pañcāgni-vidyā or the Doctrine of the ड़िवे ड़िरेस्. श्वेतकेतु, the proud son of the sage गौतम आरुणि, goes to the court of the king प्रवाहण जैवलि to exhibit his learning. However, when the king puts him five questions, he is unable to answer any of them. Crest-fallen, he returns to his ड़थेर् and objects to his not having taught this subject. Since गौतम too did not know this science, he chooses to go to the king to learn it from him. The king teaches him Pañcāgnividyā or the Doctrine of the ड़िवे ड़िरेस्. The ड़िवे ड़िरेस् are: dyuloka (heaven), parjanya (rain), this लोक or world, पुरुष (man) and yoṣā (woman). Householders who know this meditation on the ड़िवे ड़िरेस् as also the hermits who meditate with faith on the हिरण्यगर्भ go to ब्रह्मलोक by the उत्तरायण, the northern path (also called देवयान and Arcirādimārga) and will not return to this world again. But those who practise sacrifices and penances, and give gifts, will travel along the path of smoke (called Dhūmādimārga or the दक्षिणायन or पितृयान) to the पितृलोक, the world of manes. After exhausting the results of their good deeds there, they return to this world. They rotate like a Persian Wheel in the circle of transmigration, till they attain the देवयान or immediate लिबेरतिओन्. The rest, the ignorant ones, are born as moths, insects and so on.
The third section called Śrīmantha-brāhmaṇa describes the rite of Śrīmantha (the paste for prosperity) as a means to attaining greatness and thereby, wealth, which is needed to perform the Vedic rituals. There is also the eulogy of this rite and the line of teachers.
The fourth section describes the Putramantha rite, by which a होउसे-holder can get a worthy son or a worthy daughter. Only the performer of the Śrīmantha rite is eligible to conduct this rite.
The fifth, the last, section called Vaṁśa-brāhmaṇa describes the long line of teachers from हिरण्यगर्भ up to Pautimāṣīputra.
Conclusion
The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad occupies a pre-eminent place among the उपनिषद्स् not only for its size but also for its teachings. Almost all aspects of the teachings of Vedānta—Brahman/Ātman, च्रेअतिओन्, nature of the individual सोउल् and its destiny, theory of कर्म, analysis of the three states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, various modes of Upaniṣadic meditations, characteristics of a liberated being—find a place in it.
The Upaniṣad also throws some inte-resting light on the contemporary society. Not only were there, great sages and men of learning, devoted to their respective fields of knowledge, they would also meet occasionally, either for disputation or for exchange of ideas. Noble kings like जनक, प्रवाहण जैवलि and अजातशत्रु, who were themselves eminent men of learning, provided opportunities for such sages to gather in their courts and also rewarded them generously. Women, earnestly interested in Vedic learning, austerity or even self-knowledge had easy access to it, as shown by the instances of मैत्रेयी (a housewife) and Gārgī (a ब्रह्मवादिनी, student of Vedic learning). The fact that Gārgī was also one among the sages that had assembled in the court of the king जनक, and had dared to question याज्ञवल्क्य, speaks volumes about the high status of women during the Vedic period. The myth that the ancient Hindus always craved for sons and looked down upon daughters has been exploded in the मन्त्र

wherein the desire of the parents for a learned daughter (paṇḍitā duhitā) has been clearly stated.
The Upaniṣad also places frankly before us, examples of men of conceit, born out of their scholarship or high birth (eg., Dṛpta बालाकि and श्वेतकेतु) on the one hand and persons of great humility and culture who were never averse to learning from the others even though they may be inferior in the social hierarchy of those days (eg., गौतम) on the other.
References to the powerful horses of सिन्धु country, to the chariots, kings and their big retinue, cows and gold coins as also to the various kinds of spiritual sciences and rituals bespeak of a high degree of civilization and culture.
One can safely say that the Bṛhadā-raṇyaka Upaniṣad represents a landmark in the development of early philosophical literature of India.

Bṛhad-योगि-yājñavalkya
------------------------------------------
The Bṛhad-योगि-yājñavalkya is a large work in Sanskrit comprising 930 verses spread over 12 chapters. The subject matter is a combination of some topics of धर्मशास्त्रस् and of others dealt with in works on योग and mantras.
The work begins with the questions posed by some sages to Yogīśvara of मिथिला.
The following is a brief summary of the twelve chapters:
Essence of the वेदस्, the smṛtis and the fourteen vidyas; ātma-ज्ञान; mantrajapa.
Praṇava or ओङ्कार.
The व्याहृतिस् (bhūḥ etc.).
The गायत्री.
Some nyāsas (purification of limbs).
Sandhyā ritual.
Snāna (bath), तर्पण (offering of water to the manes) and जप (muttering of mantras).
Prāṇāyāma (breath control) and प्रत्याहार (withdrawal of मिन्द् from sense-objects).
Dhyāna or meditation.
Sūryopasthāna (worship of the Sun with the mantras and गायत्री).
Yogadharma or the practice of योग.
Origination of the śāstras from the वेदस् and allied topics.
The work quotes a large number of verses from the Manusmṛti and contains many verses of the Bhagavadgītā also. Several passages from the उपनिषद्स् too are found in it.
One interesting statement that this book makes is that Gārgī was the wife of याज्ञवल्क्य. This however is not correct as we find from the more authoritative scripture, viz., the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
See also YĀJÑAVALKYA and YOGI-YĀJÑAVALKYA.
